newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election campaign goes into last week.
newsitem.headline: French election campaign goes into last week.

text.p: The campaign for France's snap parliamentary election entered its last week on Saturday with the left gnawing at the lead of the ruling centre-right.

With seven days to go before campaigning ends on Friday night, the latest opinion polls saw Prime Minister Alain Juppe's conservatives likely to win a majority in the May 25-June 1 election but with a reduced majority.
A CSA survey said the RPR-UDF coalition would win 299 seats to the combined left's 256 -- a majority of 43 seats, well down on CSA's forecast of a 80-seat margin a week ago.
Another poll by the Louis Harris institute saw the conservatives and the combined left, with its ecologist allies, tied on 39 percent each.

The Louis Harris poll saw the far-right National Front polling 15 percent, unchanged from the last poll. But CSA predicted the party would not win enough in the second round of voting to gain any seats in the National Assembly.
Another burst of opinion polls was expected later in the day before a ban on publishing surveys of voters intentions in the week before voting takes effect at midnight (2200 GMT).
The ban means no more election polls will be published in France since the second round of voting, on June 1, takes place a week after the first.
"There will be no more polls from Sunday, and voters will thus have to make their decision in democratic meditation," said Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin.

As surveys indicated that 23 to 38 percent of voters were still undecided, unconfirmed reports said Gaullist President Jacques Chirac could intervene on behalf of the conservatives after returning from a state visit to China on Sunday.

Jospin said a second intervention into the campaign by Chirac, who earlier this month published a newspaper column to back the conservatives, would "distort democracy" and he would demand the right to respond.

Alarmed by reports that many conservative voters could stay away from the first round or cast blank ballots to mark their discontent over economic policies and political corruption, Juppe has warned that protest votes or abstention would favour the left and could return the Socialists after they were routed in 1993.
Foreign policy briefly burst into a campaign dominated by domestic issues on Saturday as Jospin branded the downfall of Mobutu Sese Seko a setback for the government.
"What is happening in Zaire certainly seals in a way the failure of France's African policy," he told France 2 television.
France clung to Mobutu long after other western powers had dropped him and was pushed to the diplomatic sidelines as Laurent Kabila's rebels inexorably advanced towards power.

There was no indication whether Mobutu could choose exile in France, where he owns a lluxury Riviera mansion. Analysts said Paris was unlikely to offer him shelter until after the election for fear that his presence could become a campaign issue.
Former Socialist Party chief Henri Emmanuelli seized on the sale of 30 Airbus airliners to China during Chirac's state visit to snipe at the conservatives' privatisation policies.

He told a rally that bickering conservative leaders agreed on one thing: privatisation. "And what does Jacques (Chirac) sell in China? Private sector products? Not at all. Airbus planes, the jewel of Aerospatiale, a state company," he said.
